sentences.text: The name Zuolong honors General Zuo Zongtang, combining his name with the Chinese word for dragon.
The skull of Zuolong is triangular-shaped with a snout that tapers significantly towards the end.
Large eye sockets faced the sides, and a process on the lacrimal bone formed a small crest above the eyes.
Researchers estimated that Zuolong had four premaxillary and twelve maxillary teeth in life.
The preserved teeth are D-shaped in cross-section, a trait seen in tyrannosauroids but less convex than in those groups.
The preserved skeleton includes twenty-two vertebrae from all four vertebral segments.
The manual claws are strongly curved and feature lateral grooves along their length.
The hip bones display a supraacetabular crest extending from the posterior end of the acetabulum.
The genus Zuolong was described by Choiniere et al. in 2010, with the type species Zuolong salleei.
The holotype fossil was discovered in 2001 in the upper part of the Shishugou Formation near Wucaiwan, Xinjiang, China.
The specimen was found in 2001 but was not formally described until 2010.
The holotype specimen IVPP V15912 includes a partially complete skull and many post-cranial bones.
Gregory S. Paul hypothesized that the holotype is a juvenile and estimated an adult length of 3 meters and a mass of 50 kg.
Some authors suggest an adult Zuolong reached a length of 3.35 meters and a mass of 43 kg.
Thomas R. Holtz Jr. considers the holotype specimen to almost certainly belong to a juvenile theropod.
The most common hypothesis regarding Zuolong's taxonomy is that it is a basal member of Coelurosauria.
Later studies, including a 2020 description of Aratasaurus, a 2022 phylogeny by Rolando and colleagues, and a 2024 study by Andrea Cau, included Zuolong in their analyses.
Zuolong lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic period, between 161 and 155 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
The time range for Zuolong is the Oxfordian stage, from 161.5 to 154.8 million years ago.
It is debated whether the implications of Zuolong's discovery as one of the oldest known coelurosaurs can be fully understood without more fossil material.
Xing and colleagues suggest that the discrepancy between their ontogeny and conventional analyses highlights the need for more specimens to confidently establish phylogenetic relationships.
